claim: All chromosomes in the Drosophila obscura group lineage were ancestrally telocentric.
source: All chromosomes in this lineage were ancestrally telocentric and the creation of metacentric chromosomes in some species was driven by de novo seeding of new centromeres at ancestrally gene-rich regions, independently of chromosomal rearrangements.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on the genomic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The creation of metacentric chromosomes in some Drosophila obscura group species was driven by de novo seeding of new centromeres at ancestrally gene-rich regions.
source: All chromosomes in this lineage were ancestrally telocentric and the creation of metacentric chromosomes in some species was driven by de novo seeding of new centromeres at ancestrally gene-rich regions, independently of chromosomal rearrangements.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on genomic analysis and synteny comparisons.

claim: The creation of metacentric chromosomes occurred independently of chromosomal rearrangements.
source: All chromosomes in this lineage were ancestrally telocentric and the creation of metacentric chromosomes in some species was driven by de novo seeding of new centromeres at ancestrally gene-rich regions, independently of chromosomal rearrangements.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on synteny analysis showing no evidence of pericentric inversions in most cases.

claim: The emergence of centromeres resulted in a drastic size increase due to repeat accumulation.
source: The emergence of centromeres resulted in a drastic size increase due to repeat accumulation, and dozens of genes previously located in euchromatin are now embedded in pericentromeric heterochromatin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by genomic data showing size expansion of pericentromeric regions.

claim: Dozens of genes previously located in euchromatin are now embedded in pericentromeric heterochromatin.
source: The emergence of centromeres resulted in a drastic size increase due to repeat accumulation, and dozens of genes previously located in euchromatin are now embedded in pericentromeric heterochromatin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by synteny analysis and H3K9me3 enrichment data.

claim: Metacentric chromosomes secondarily became telocentric in the pseudoobscura subgroup through centromere repositioning and a pericentric inversion.
source: Metacentric chromosomes secondarily became telocentric in the pseudoobscura subgroup through centromere repositioning and a pericentric inversion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on synteny analysis and genomic comparisons.

claim: Former (peri)centric sequences shrunk dramatically in size after their inactivation.
source: The former (peri)centric sequences left behind shrunk dramatically in size after their inactivation, yet contain remnants of their evolutionary past, including increased repeat-content and heterochromatic environment.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by genomic size comparisons of paleocentromeres.

claim: Inactivated (peri)centric sequences contain remnants of their evolutionary past, including increased repeat-content and heterochromatic environment.
source: The former (peri)centric sequences left behind shrunk dramatically in size after their inactivation, yet contain remnants of their evolutionary past, including increased repeat-content and heterochromatic environment.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by repeat content analysis and H3K9me3 enrichment data.

claim: Centromere movements are accompanied by rapid turnover of the major satellite DNA detected in (peri)centromeric regions.
source: Centromere movements are accompanied by rapid turnover of the major satellite DNA detected in (peri)centromeric regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by satellite DNA identification and FISH experiments.

claim: Centromeres consist of species-specific kilobase- to megabase-sized arrays of tandem repeats in many eukaryotes.
source: In many eukaryotes, centromeres consist of species-specific kilobase- to megabase-sized arrays of tandem repeats (Willard, 1990; Birchler et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009; Melters et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Centromeres are characterized by a distinct type of chromatin where histone H3 is replaced by a centromere-specific histone H3 variant (cenH3).
source: Centromeres are characterized by a distinct type of chromatin where histone H3 is replaced by a centromere-specific histone H3 variant (cenH3) (Karpen and Allshire, 1997; Allshire and Karpen, 2008), which interacts with other proteins to seed the kinetochore.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: cenH3 interacts with other proteins to seed the kinetochore.
source: Centromeres are characterized by a distinct type of chromatin where histone H3 is replaced by a centromere-specific histone H3 variant (cenH3) (Karpen and Allshire, 1997; Allshire and Karpen, 2008), which interacts with other proteins to seed the kinetochore.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In budding yeast, characteristic sequences of ~120 bp fully specify centromere identity.
source: In budding yeast, characteristic sequences of ~120 bp fully specify centromere identity (Hieter et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In organisms with complex repetitive centromeres, the site of kinetochore assembly is not strictly governed by primary DNA sequence but appears to be epigenetically determined.
source: In organisms with complex repetitive centromeres, the site of kinetochore assembly is not strictly governed by primary DNA sequence but appears to be epigenetically determined (Karpen and Allshire, 1997; Allshire and Karpen, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The key-determining factor in epigenetic centromere specification is the deposition of the centromere-specific histone H3 variant cenH3.
source: The key-determining factor in epigenetic centromere specification is the deposition of the centromere-specific histone H3 variant cenH3 (also known as CENP-A).
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about centromere specification.

claim: Neo-centromeres form at ectopic chromosomal loci in many species.
source: The concept of epigenetic specification of the centromere is further supported by the existence of neo-centromeres, which form at ectopic chromosomal loci in many species (du Sart et al., 1997) and lack shared sequence features (Burrack and Berman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Neo-centromeres lack shared sequence features.
source: The concept of epigenetic specification of the centromere is further supported by the existence of neo-centromeres, which form at ectopic chromosomal loci in many species (du Sart et al., 1997) and lack shared sequence features (Burrack and Berman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Both the centromeric histone protein (cenH3) and the underlying DNA sequence that forms the centromere vary among species.
source: Both the centromeric histone protein (cenH3, which is called Cid in Drosophila), as well as the underlying DNA sequence that forms the centromere (that is, the centromeric satellite DNA) vary among species (Henikoff et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The position of centromeres along the chromosome varies widely and results in diverse karyotypes across species.
source: In addition to their primary sequence, the position of centromeres along the chromosome varies widely as well and results in diverse karyotypes across species (The Tree of Sex Consortium, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Changes in centromere position can be driven by chromosomal re-arrangements or by evolutionary centromere repositioning.
source: Changes in centromere position can be driven by chromosomal re-arrangements, moving an existing centromere to a new location, or by evolutionary centromere repositioning – a move of the centromere along the chromosome not accompanied by structural rearrangements (Ferreri et al., 2005; Carbone et al., 2006; Rocchi et al., 2012; Schubert, 2018; Nishimura et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ancestral karyotype of Drosophila consists of five large telocentric chromosomes (rods) and the much smaller dot chromosome.
source: The ancestral karyotype of Drosophila consists of five large telocentric chromosomes (rods; termed Muller elements A-E) and the much smaller dot chromosome (Muller F), and novel karyotypes have originated repeatedly by chromosomal fusions and inversions.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about Drosophila karyotypes.

claim: Novel karyotypes in Drosophila have originated repeatedly by chromosomal fusions and inversions.
source: The ancestral karyotype of Drosophila consists of five large telocentric chromosomes (rods; termed Muller elements A-E) and the much smaller dot chromosome (Muller F), and novel karyotypes have originated repeatedly by chromosomal fusions and inversions.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about Drosophila karyotype evolution.

claim: The ancestral karyotype of the obscura group consists of five ancestral telocentric rods and the dot chromosome.
source: The ancestral karyotype (found in flies of the subobscura group) consists of five ancestral telocentric rods and the dot chromosome, while species in the obscura and affinis group mainly contain metacentric chromosomes, and most chromosomes in the pseudoobscura group are telocentric.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic inference and karyotype data.

claim: Species in the obscura and affinis group mainly contain metacentric chromosomes.
source: The ancestral karyotype (found in flies of the subobscura group) consists of five ancestral telocentric rods and the dot chromosome, while species in the obscura and affinis group mainly contain metacentric chromosomes, and most chromosomes in the pseudoobscura group are telocentric.
evidence: This is based on karyotype data from the manuscript and literature.

claim: Most chromosomes in the pseudoobscura group are telocentric.
source: The ancestral karyotype (found in flies of the subobscura group) consists of five ancestral telocentric rods and the dot chromosome, while species in the obscura and affinis group mainly contain metacentric chromosomes, and most chromosomes in the pseudoobscura group are telocentric.
evidence: This is based on karyotype data from the manuscript and literature.

claim: Long-read sequencing allows assembly of entire chromosomes, including pericentromeric regions.
source: Long-read sequencing allows assembly of entire chromosomes, including pericentromeric regions
evidence: This is demonstrated by the assembly results presented in the manuscript.

claim: A combination of PacBio and Nanopore sequencing and Hi-C scaffolding was used to generate highly contiguous genome assemblies.
source: We used a combination of PacBio and Nanopore sequencing and Hi-C scaffolding to generate highly contiguous genome assemblies of high quality for D. pseudoobscura, D. athabasca, D. subobscura and D. lowei (Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2, see Materials and methods and Appendix 1).
evidence: This describes the methods used in the study.

claim: Chromosome-level assemblies contain large stretches of repetitive DNA, including pericentromere and putative centromere sequence.
source: For each species, we were able to generate chromosome-level assemblies that contain large stretches of repetitive DNA, including pericentromere and putative centromere sequence (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the assembly results and figures showing repeat content.

claim: Euchromatic regions from each chromosome were typically assembled into just a few contigs.
source: In particular, euchromatic regions from each chromosome were typically assembled into just a few contigs (Table 1, Figure 2), and Hi-C scaffolding allowed for the orientation and placement of these contigs into chromosome-level assemblies (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the assembly statistics in Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: BUSCO scores reveal that the genomes are highly complete.
source: BUSCO (Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs) scores reveal that our genomes are highly complete (Supplementary file 3) and match or exceed other recently published high quality Drosophila genomes (Mahajan et al., 2018; Puerma et al., 2018; Puerma et al., 2018; Karageorgiou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on BUSCO analysis results.

claim: The chromosome-level genome assemblies are in agreement with the karyotypes based on cytology.
source: Our chromosome-level genome assemblies are in agreement with the karyotypes based on cytology (Buzzati-Traverso and Scossiroli, 1955; see Figures 1–3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison with cytological data and shown in the figures.

claim: D. subobscura has five large telocentric chromosomes.
source: Our Hi-C scaffolding maps reconstruct five large telocentric chromosomes in D. subobscura, three large metacentric and two telocentric chromosomes in D. athabasca, two large metacentric and three telocentric chromosomes in D. lowei and four large telocentric and one metacentric chromosome in D. pseudoobscura and D. miranda (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Hi-C scaffolding results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: D. athabasca has three large metacentric and two telocentric chromosomes.
source: Our Hi-C scaffolding maps reconstruct five large telocentric chromosomes in D. subobscura, three large metacentric and two telocentric chromosomes in D. athabasca, two large metacentric and three telocentric chromosomes in D. lowei and four large telocentric and one metacentric chromosome in D. pseudoobscura and D. miranda (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Hi-C scaffolding results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: D. lowei has two large metacentric and three telocentric chromosomes.
source: Our Hi-C scaffolding maps reconstruct five large telocentric chromosomes in D. subobscura, three large metacentric and two telocentric chromosomes in D. athabasca, two large metacentric and three telocentric chromosomes in D. lowei and four large telocentric and one metacentric chromosome in D. pseudoobscura and D. miranda (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Hi-C scaffolding results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: D. pseudoobscura has four large telocentric and one metacentric chromosome.
source: Our Hi-C scaffolding maps reconstruct five large telocentric chromosomes in D. subobscura, three large metacentric and two telocentric chromosomes in D. athabasca, two large metacentric and three telocentric chromosomes in D. lowei and four large telocentric and one metacentric chromosome in D. pseudoobscura and D. miranda (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Hi-C scaffolding results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: D. miranda has four large telocentric and one metacentric chromosome.
source: Our Hi-C scaffolding maps reconstruct five large telocentric chromosomes in D. subobscura, three large metacentric and two telocentric chromosomes in D. athabasca, two large metacentric and three telocentric chromosomes in D. lowei and four large telocentric and one metacentric chromosome in D. pseudoobscura and D. miranda (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Hi-C scaffolding results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A 21 bp motif and a 99 bp motif are the most abundant tandem repeats in D. miranda.
source: We previously annotated satellites in the D. miranda genome and recovered two repeats, a 21 bp motif and a 99 bp motif that were the most abundant tandem repeats (Mahajan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on previous analysis cited in the manuscript.

claim: Both the 21 bp and 99 bp satellites were enriched at the putative centromere of each chromosome in D. miranda.
source: Both of these satellites were enriched at the putative centromere of each chromosome in our assembly and had sequence characteristics of typical centromere satellites (Mahajan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on previous analysis cited in the manuscript.

claim: The 21 bp motif is found in D. pseudoobscura with an 84-mer being the most common higher order variant.
source: We identify the same 21 bp motif in D. pseudoobscura (again with an 84-mer being the most common higher order variant, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the TRF analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The 99 bp motif is absent in D. pseudoobscura.
source: Intriguingly, however, we fail to detect the 99 bp motif in D. pseudoobscura, both when probing for abundant satellites, and when searching the genome directly for the 99-mer.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the D. pseudoobscura genome.

claim: A higher-order variant of the 21-mer (a 63-mer) is found in D. lowei.
source: Similarly, we find a higher-order variant of the 21-mer in D. lowei (a 63-mer; Figure 4A), and only a distantly related 99-mer on Muller A-AD (mean = 18.1% sequence divergence).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the TRF analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: FISH hybridization confirms that both the 21-mer and the 99-mer are enriched around the centromeres in D. miranda.
source: Indeed, we find both the 21-mer and the 99-mer enriched around the centromeres in D. miranda (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FISH experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FISH in D. pseudoobscura only showed strong staining for the 21-mer around its centromeres but failed to detect any signal for the 99-mer.
source: In contrast, FISH with the same probes in D. pseudoobscura only showed strong staining for the 21-mer around its centromeres but we failed to detect any signal for the 99-mer (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FISH experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A 160 bp motif is the most abundant repeat unit in the D. athabasca genome.
source: In the D. athabasca genome, we identify a 160 bp motif as the most abundant repeat unit (Figure 4A), and this motif is enriched in the assembled (peri)centromere in both telocentric and metacentric chromosomes (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the TRF analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4B.

claim: FISH experiments confirm that the 160 bp satellite is localized to the centromeric region on all chromosomes except Muller F in D. athabasca.
source: FISH experiments again confirm our bioinformatics approach and demonstrate that the 160 bp satellite is localized to the centromeric region on all chromosomes except Muller F (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FISH experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A 12 bp satellite is highly enriched in raw Illumina whole genome sequencing reads of D. subobscura and yet appears largely absent from the assembly.
source: Computational identification and quantification of short tandemly repeating sequences using k-Seek revealed a 12 bp satellite that is highly enriched in raw Illumina whole genome sequencing reads of D. subobscura and yet appears largely absent from our assembly (or from D. guanche and all other species; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by k-Seek analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: FISH analysis confirms that the 12 bp repeat is enriched at all the centromeres of D. subobscura chromosomes, except Muller F.
source: FISH analysis confirms that the 12 bp repeat is enriched at all the centromeres of D. suboboscura chromosomes, except Muller F (and our genomic analysis suggests that the 107-mer is a good candidate for the centromere-associated repeat on Muller F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FISH experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The pericentromere on D. pseudoobscura Muller A is roughly 14.1 Mb and contains 42 genes with orthologs in D. subobscura.
source: The pericentromere on D. pseudoobscura Muller A is roughly 14.1 Mb (Table 1) and contains 42 genes with orthologs in D. subobscura (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and synteny comparisons shown in Table 1 and Figure 5.

claim: The 42 genes in the pericentromere of D. pseudoobscura Muller A are found in two 'seed regions' on Muller A in D. subobscura, whose combined size is 0.3 Mb.
source: These genes are found in two 'seed regions' on Muller A in D. subobscura, whose combined size is 0.3 Mb.
evidence: This is based on synteny analysis comparing D. pseudoobscura and D. subobscura.

claim: The pericentromere of Muller B in D. athabasca is roughly 22.8 Mb and contains 93 pericentromere genes that are conserved in D. subobscura and found in two seed regions with a total size of 0.66 Mb.
source: Similarly, the pericentromere of Muller B in D. athabasca is roughly 22.8 Mb, and we identify 93 pericentromere genes that are conserved in D. subobscura and found in two seed regions with a total size of 0.66 Mb.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and synteny comparisons.

claim: The pericentromere on D. athabasca Muller E is roughly 11.2 Mb with 73 conserved genes in two seed regions of D. subobscura with 0.88 Mb in size.
source: Finally, the pericentromere on D. athabasca Muller E is roughly 11.2 Mb with 73 conserved genes in two seed regions of D. subobscura with 0.88 Mb in size.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and synteny comparisons.

claim: The combined assembled pericentromers in the metacentric Muller A, B and E are ~48.1 Mb, while the orthologous regions in D. subobscura are only ~1.81 Mb in size (i.e. a total increase over 27-fold).
source: Thus, the combined assembled pericentromers in the metacentric Muller A, B and E are ~48.1 Mb (Table 1), while the orthologous regions in D. subobscura are only ~1.81 Mb in size (i.e. a total increase over 27-fold).
evidence: This is based on genomic size comparisons between species.

claim: The majority of the genes previously located in the metacentric pericentromere remain on the chromosome arm after the shift in centromere position in the pseudoobscura subgroup.
source: Comparisons of gene content between species reveal that the majority of the genes previously located in the metacentric pericentromere remain on the chromosome arm after this shift in centromere position happened (Figure 3B, Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synteny analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 5.

claim: While the pericentromere of Muller B in D. athabasca is 22.8 Mb, most homologous genes in D. pseudoobscura are located in a 0.8 Mb sized region in the center of Muller B (58 genes) and almost all remaining genes are found in the pericentromere (22 genes).
source: Specifically, while the pericentromere of Muller B in D. athabasca is 22.8 Mb, most homologous genes in D. pseudoobscura are located in a 0.8 Mb sized region in the center of Muller B (58 genes) and almost all remaining genes are found in the pericentromere (22 genes).
evidence: This is based on synteny analysis and genomic size comparisons.

claim: The homologous genes in the 11.2 Mb large pericentromere on D. athabasca Muller E are found in two segments along the homologous chromosome in D. pseudoobscura (they are roughly 0.96 Mb and 0.18 Mb in size and contain 58 and 12 genes).
source: Likewise, the homologous genes in the 11.2 Mb large pericentromere on D. athabasca Muller E are found in two segments along the homologous chromosome in D. pseudoobscura (they are roughly 0.96 Mb and 0.18 Mb in size and contain 58 and 12 genes).
evidence: This is based on synteny analysis and genomic size comparisons.

claim: The repeat content in paleocentromeres is still increased above background levels, despite their massive reduction in size.
source: As a mark of their evolutionary past, we find that the repeat content in paleocentromeres is still increased above background levels, despite their massive reduction in size.
evidence: This is based on repeat content analysis of paleocentromeres.

claim: In D. pseudoobscura, the repeat content in euchromatic DNA (that is, non-pericentromere) is ~6%; in the paleocentromeres,~18% of DNA is masked for repeats on Muller B and ~32% on Muller E.
source: In D. pseudoobscura, for example, the repeat content in euchromatic DNA (that is, non-pericentromere) is ~6%; in the paleocentromeres,~18% of DNA is masked for repeats on Muller B and ~32% on Muller E (Figure 2; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on repeat masking analysis shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Paleocentromere islands on both Muller B and E show a clear spike in heterochromatin enrichment (as measured by H3K9me3 profiles).
source: In addition, paleocentromere islands on both Muller elements show a clear spike in heterochromatin enrichment (as measured by H3K9me3 profiles, see Figure 2; Mahajan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated by H3K9me3 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The subobscura subgroup split from the other species groups about 20MY ago.
source: Molecular dating in this species group suggests that the subobscura subgroup split from the other species groups about 20MY ago (Gao et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on molecular dating from a cited study.

claim: The affinis and pseudoobscura subgroups split from the obscura flies about 16MY ago and diverged from each other roughly 14MY ago.
source: The affinis and pseudoobscura subgroups split from the obscura flies about 16MY ago and diverged from each other roughly 14MY ago (Gao et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on molecular dating from a cited study.

claim: D. lowei diverged about 9MY ago.
source: D. lowei diverged about 9MY ago, and D. miranda and D. pseudoobscura split roughly 3MY ago (Gao et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on molecular dating from a cited study.

claim: D. miranda and D. pseudoobscura split roughly 3MY ago.
source: D. lowei diverged about 9MY ago, and D. miranda and D. pseudoobscura split roughly 3MY ago (Gao et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on molecular dating from a cited study.

claim: Muller A, B and E all became metacentric 16-20MY ago.
source: These rough time estimates suggest that Muller A, B and E all became metacentric 16-20MY ago.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic dating and karyotype reconstruction.

claim: Muller A and D subsequently fused 14-16MY ago.
source: Muller A and D subsequently fused (14-16MY ago), and Muller B reverted to a telocentric chromosome 9-14MY ago, while Muller E shifted its centromere only 3-9MY ago.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic dating and karyotype reconstruction.

claim: Muller B reverted to a telocentric chromosome 9-14MY ago.
source: Muller A and D subsequently fused (14-16MY ago), and Muller B reverted to a telocentric chromosome 9-14MY ago, while Muller E shifted its centromere only 3-9MY ago.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic dating and karyotype reconstruction.

claim: Muller E shifted its centromere only 3-9MY ago.
source: Muller A and D subsequently fused (14-16MY ago), and Muller B reverted to a telocentric chromosome 9-14MY ago, while Muller E shifted its centromere only 3-9MY ago.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic dating and karyotype reconstruction.

claim: The pericentromeric regions on each of the three metacentric chromosomes are largely syntenic with a small number of euchromatic regions in D. subobscura that have a similar number and orientation of genes.
source: Intriguingly, the pericentromeric regions on each of the three metacentric chromosomes are largely syntenic with a small number of euchromatic regions in D. subobscura that have a similar number and orientation of genes.
evidence: This is based on synteny analysis comparing metacentric and telocentric chromosomes.

claim: Novel pericentromeres were seeded in previously gene-dense regions on Muller A, B and E, and dramatically extended in size by the accumulation of repetitive DNA.
source: As suggested by our broad-scale synteny comparisons (Figure 3B), this more fine-scale look confirms that novel pericentromeres were seeded in previously gene-dense regions on Muller A, B and E, and dramatically extended in size by the accumulation of repetitive DNA (see Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synteny analysis and genomic size comparisons shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The homologs of genes found in the pericentromere of D. athabasca (or D. lowei) are all located along the euchromatic chromatin arm in both D. miranda and D. pseudoobscura, mega-bases away from the centromere on Muller E.
source: Homologs of genes found in the pericentromere of D. athabasca (or D. lowei) are all located along the euchromatic chromatin arm in both D. miranda and D. pseudoobscura, mega-bases away from the centromere on Muller E (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synteny analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: A pericentric inversion was involved in the transition of a metacentric Muller B to a telocentric chromosome in the pseudoobcura group.
source: Thus, these syntenic relationships suggest that a pericentric inversion was involved in the transition of a metacentric Muller B to a telocentric chromosome in the pseudoobcura group.
evidence: This is inferred from synteny analysis showing that some pericentric genes are shared between metacentric and telocentric forms.

claim: The genomic regions in D. subobscura that became incorporated into the pericentromeres in D. athabasca and the pseudoobscura subgroup (i.e. the pericentromere 'seed' regions) overall look like random, anonymous regions in D. subobscura.
source: The genomic regions in D. subobscura that became incorporated into the pericentromeres in D. athabasca and the pseudoobscura subgroup (i.e. the pericentromere 'seed' regions) overall look like random, anonymous regions in D. subobscura (Figure 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene density and repeat content in seed regions shown in Figure 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The most unusual aspect of each of these seeds regions is that they are very AT-rich.
source: The most unusual aspect of each of these seeds regions is that they are very AT-rich (Figure 5B; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GC content analysis shown in Figure 5B and Supplementary file 7.

claim: AT content is significantly increased for each functional category (intergenic, genic and exon regions) in seed regions, relative to genomic background.
source: Interestingly, we find that AT content is significantly increased for each functional category in seed regions, relative to genomic background (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of AT content shown in Supplementary file 7.

claim: Genes located on the chromosome arms outside the pericentromeric region generally show no enrichment of H3K9me3.
source: As expected, genes located on the chromosome arms outside the pericentromeric region generally show no enrichment of H3K9me3 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metagene plots of H3K9me3 enrichment shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Genes on the dot chromosome have a unique chromatin structure with H3K9me3 strongly enriched over gene bodies.
source: In contrast, the small dot chromosome of Drosophila is heterochromatic yet gene-rich, and genes on this chromosome have adopted a unique chromatin structure (Riddle et al., 2012). While there is a depletion of repressive chromatin marks at their transcription start site, H3K9me3 is strongly enriched over gene bodies (Riddle et al., 2012), and this unique chromatin signature is regulated by a molecular pathway unique to the dot chromosome.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Genes in the neo-centromeres of D. athabasca show a unique chromatin signature: H3K9me3 levels are depleted at their transcription start site and across their gene body, yet H3K9me3 levels are strikingly elevated at flanking regions.
source: Genes in the neo-centromeres of D. athabasca show a unique chromatin signature: H3K9me3 levels are depleted at their transcription start site and across their gene body, yet H3K9me3 levels are strikingly elevated at flanking regions (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metagene plots of H3K9me3 enrichment shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There is no reduction in expression levels of genes within pericentromeric regions of metacentric chromosomes in D. athabasca relative to genes located in neighboring euchromatin.
